title: Making Your Home More Sensory-Friendly
body:
Every autistic person's sensory profile is different, so the goal isn't to follow a checklist exactly but to notice what seems to overwhelm or soothe your specific child, then adjust the environment around that.

Lighting is often a good place to start. Harsh overhead fluorescent lighting bothers many autistic people; swapping to warmer, dimmable bulbs or adding lamps for softer ambient light can reduce a source of constant low-level stress. Blackout curtains help if bright daylight or streetlights are an issue at bedtime.

Sound matters just as much. A designated quiet space — even a corner with cushions and noise-reducing headphones available — gives your child somewhere to retreat when things get loud. Rugs, curtains, and soft furnishings can reduce echo and background noise in hard-surfaced rooms.

Touch and texture are easy to overlook. Scratchy tags, certain fabrics, or specific textures on furniture can be a constant irritant. Letting your child choose bedding, clothing fabric, and even where they sit can remove friction you might not otherwise notice.

Predictability is a sensory tool too. Visual schedules, consistent furniture placement, and giving a heads-up before changing a room's layout all reduce the cognitive load of an unpredictable environment.

Finally, involve your child in the process where possible — ask what feels too bright, too loud, or too itchy. Older children and teens are often the best source of information about their own sensory needs.
